lead: A transformer moves AC power from one coil to another through an iron core, with no moving parts. Both coils share one alternating flux, so each turn gets the same induced EMF. Hence voltage ratio equals turns ratio, current ratio is its inverse, and power passes almost unchanged. Transformers sit at power stations, substations and inside phone chargers.
prereq: You need 3.1 for the iron core as a magnetic circuit, 3.2 for mutual inductance, and Unit 2 for RMS value and form factor.

blocks.text: A transformer has two coils on one closed iron core. The supply coil is the primary; the load coil is the secondary. Power crosses by mutual inductance; nothing moves. The core is stacked from 0.35–0.5 mm silicon-steel sheets, varnished to make a laminated core. Laminations break eddy-current paths, cutting eddy loss; silicon raises resistivity and cuts hysteresis loss. The core is the magnetic circuit of 3.1 with no air gap.

In core type, windings sit on vertical limbs and the iron forms one loop. In shell type, the core wraps the windings and flux splits into two outer paths. Core type suits high voltage; shell type is stronger and common in small units. The low-voltage winding sits next to the core, high-voltage outside: less insulation, better cooling.

sections.h3: Working principle and the EMF equation

blocks.text: Connect the primary to AC. Primary current makes an alternating flux in the core. That flux links both windings, so every turn, primary or secondary, gets the same EMF. That one fact decides the design.

items: Flux is sinusoidal: Φ = Φm sin(ωt), with peak Φm in Wb and ω = 2πf.
For N turns in series: E = 4.44 f N Φm.

blocks.where: E is RMS induced EMF in volts; f is supply frequency in Hz; N is turns; Φm is peak core flux in Wb; 4.44 = 4 × 1.11, the sine form factor times the half-cycle average 4fΦm.

blocks.text: The 4.44 is 4 × 1.11. Flux swings from −Φm to +Φm in half a cycle, giving average EMF per turn 4fΦm. The sine form factor 1.11 makes it RMS. It is a property of the sine wave, not the transformer.

The primary EMF opposes the supply, so it is a counter EMF. At no load it almost equals supply voltage; net voltage across primary resistance is tiny, so only small magnetising current flows. On load, secondary current weakens flux, counter EMF drops, and primary current rises to restore flux. Primary current follows the load.

sections.h3: Turns ratio, kVA rating and losses

blocks.text: Divide the secondary EMF equation by the primary: E₁/E₂ = N₁/N₂, the turns ratio. N₂ > N₁ is step-up; N₂ < N₁ is step-down. An ideal transformer has no winding resistance, leakage flux or iron loss, so input power equals output power and I₂/I₁ = N₁/N₂.

blocks.where: Subscripts 1 and 2 are primary and secondary; all values are RMS; the transformer is ideal.

blocks.text: A real transformer is rated in kVA, not kW: its limit is winding current and insulation voltage, not load phase angle. A 100 kVA unit delivers 100 kVA at power factor 1 or 0.8, but different kW.

items: Copper loss = I²R in windings; it rises with load current.
Iron loss = hysteresis + eddy loss; roughly constant at fixed voltage and frequency.
Transmission uses step-up transformers (Unit 6): high voltage, low current, lower I²R line loss.
A phone charger is a small step-down unit; a welding set uses a step-down transformer with loose coupling for low voltage at large adjustable current.

examples.question: A single-phase transformer is rated 230 V / 23 V, 50 Hz, and its primary has 460 turns. (a) Find the secondary turns. (b) Find the peak core flux. (c) If the secondary supplies 2 A, find the primary current, treating the transformer as ideal.
steps: Given: V₁ = 230 V, V₂ = 23 V, f = 50 Hz, N₁ = 460 turns, I₂ = 2 A.
examples.answer: N₂ = 46 turns, peak core flux Φm = 2.25 mWb, and primary current I₁ = 0.2 A.
examples.check:
N1 = 460
V1 = 230.0
V2 = 23.0
f = 50.0
I2 = 2.0
N2 = N1 * V2 / V1
Phi = V1 / (4.44 * f * N1)
I1 = I2 * V2 / V1
print(round(N2, 2))
print(round(Phi * 1000, 2))
print(round(I1, 3))

examples.question: A 50 Hz transformer has 200 primary turns and is connected to a 230 V supply. Find the peak core flux.
steps: Given: V₁ = 230 V, f = 50 Hz, N₁ = 200 turns.
examples.answer: The peak core flux is 5.18 mWb.

traps: Putting RMS voltage into E = 4.44 f N Φm and calling Φm RMS. Φm is always peak; RMS flux is Φm/√2.
Writing 4 instead of 4.44. 4 gives average EMF per turn; the 1.11 form factor makes it RMS.
Inverting the current ratio. Voltage ratio is N₁/N₂; current ratio is N₂/N₁; a step-up steps current down.
Assuming kVA rating falls with load power factor. Rating is fixed by winding current and insulation; only kW changes.
Thinking primary current is set by primary resistance. It is set by load: more secondary current gives more primary current to restore flux.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of laminating the core of a transformer?
quiz.a: Laminations break eddy-current paths in the iron, so eddy current loss and core heating fall.

quiz.q: Why does a transformer draw only a small current from the supply when the secondary is open?
quiz.a: The primary counter EMF almost equals supply voltage. Net voltage across primary resistance is small, so only small magnetising current flows.

quiz.q: Why is a transformer rated in kVA and not in kW?
quiz.a: Heating is set by winding current; insulation by voltage. Both are independent of load phase angle, so rating is rated voltage × rated current = kVA.

quiz.q: A 50 Hz transformer has 200 primary turns and is fed from a 230 V supply. Find the peak core flux.
A transformer with 1200 primary turns works on 240 V, 50 Hz. Find the secondary turns for a 12 V output, and the primary current when the secondary supplies 5 A (ideal transformer).
A transformer rated 230 V / 23 V is connected to a 230 V DC supply instead of AC. Predict what happens and give the reason.
quiz.a: Flux stays constant, dΦ/dt = 0, so no counter EMF appears. Primary current is limited only by small winding resistance, so the winding overheats and burns. A transformer cannot work on steady DC.

quiz.q: The core flux of a transformer stays almost constant from no load to full load at rated voltage. Explain why, using the EMF equation.
quiz.a: E = 4.44 f N Φm and the primary counter EMF nearly equals fixed supply voltage. With f and N fixed, Φm stays nearly constant. Primary current rises only enough to restore flux weakened by secondary current.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real transformers use an equivalent circuit with winding resistance, leakage reactance and a magnetising branch; machines courses use it for regulation and efficiency. Switching on can draw large inrush current for a few cycles if the core saturates on the first flux peak. Amorphous-metal cores and cast-resin dry-type units are used where eddy loss or fire risk matters. On the grid, on-load tap changers adjust turns ratio in steps to hold voltage as load varies. Search next for "transformer equivalent circuit", "inrush current" and "on-load tap changer".
